summary: Emergence and 49 Palms set out a 2x2 for AI pricing on autonomy and attribution. title: The AI pricing and monetization playbook
author: Atlas Editors
summary: Bessemer's playbook frames three AI business models (copilots, agents, AI-enabled services) and three charge metrics (consumption, workflow, outcome), trading cost predictability for value alignment as you move toward outcomes. It says AI companies see 50-60% gross margins versus 80-90% for SaaS because COGS matter again, and recommends hybrid base subscription plus usage or outcome tiers when uncertain. Intercom Fin at $0.99 per resolution is the anchor outcome example, and the piece says outcome contracts reshape AE deal sizing, CS incentives and require forward-deployed engineers. It warns of a 2026 renewal cliff for soft-ROI copilots and lists outcome-priced examples including EvenUp, Graph AI, Leena AI and Resolve AI.

title: You are not a model. Don't price per token.
author: Tugce Erten and Sarah Wang
summary: a16z growth partners Tugce Erten and Sarah Wang argue applications should not import model-layer token pricing, and should instead price at the highest layer of value they can reliably measure, attribute and defend. Model access is priced in tokens, useful work in recognizable units often packaged as credits, and clear attributable business results as outcomes. In a survey of 50 technical AI buyers, 27 preferred credits tied to recognizable work and 14 preferred tokens. Good credit systems separate what the work is worth from what it costs, which protects margin and lets the vendor keep part of falling model costs; Clay is cited as splitting Data Credits, Actions and token pass-through. Outcomes such as a resolved conversation, processed claim or recovered dollar should be priced once they are observable, attributable and valuable enough for a stable price, often inside hybrids.

key_facts.quote: price at the highest layer of value that they can reliably measure, attribute, and defend
In our survey of 50 technical AI buyers, 27 preferred credits tied to recognizable work, while only 14 preferred tokens.
Once the outcome becomes observable, attributable, and valuable enough to support a stable price, the meter should move again.

title: The $1.5 trillion Services-as-Software opportunity (HFS)
summary: HFS sizes Services-as-Software as a $1.5T opportunity where services are codified as software. Data note: analyst marketing excerpt; full report gated.

key_facts.quote: $1.5 trillion opportunity

takeaways: $1.5T is a top-down ceiling for services-software convergence, not a spend number (Q4)
excerpt:
Enterprise leaders can no longer treat services and software as distinct buying categories. Earlier this year, HFS sized the Software-as-Services (SaS) market as a $1.5 trillion opportunity. title: nasscom Conversations: Why Most AI Projects Fail in Enterprises? Rohan Murty Explains
summary: Rohan Murty, founder of Workfabric, argues that despite agent hype the core truth is that agents only succeed in a few areas such as code generation and perhaps some legal work, and that most functions have no successful agents producing ROI. His reason is that models generalize well but do not understand the local context of the organization they serve. Workfabric's platform, Context Fabric, captures context from how people interact with their devices using edge models, then assembles it in the cloud on GPUs, for example combining what delivery, support and legal teams learn about a customer into proactive pitches for sales. He says the future of traditional IT services, excluding BPO, shifts from writing code for microprocessors to shipping context to models, and that when intelligence is democratized an organization's context is what differentiates it. He expects AI to disrupt some human labor and intermediaries such as analyst firms.

summary: LangChain co-founder and CEO Harrison Chase defines an agent as a harness that orchestrates a model and context, and says owning your intelligence means owning all three, including the ability to switch models to avoid lock-in. Every agent is essentially an LLM running in a loop calling tools, and LangChain's Deep Agents, a model-agnostic, more general-purpose take on Claude Code, customizes that loop with middleware for summarization, context offloading, sandboxes, file systems, sub-agents and memory, plus model profiles that swap file-edit implementations per model. He stresses private evals (Harbor as an emerging open-source standard), observability because bad context more often than weak models causes failures, and a trace-driven data flywheel, now automated by LangSmith Engine, an agent that turns traces into issues and proposed harness fixes. He does not know whether harnesses will converge.

title: AI Engineer: Is the Agent Harness Dead? (Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI)
summary: Jediah Katz, longest-tenured engineer on Cursor's agent harness and now at SpaceXAI after what he describes as SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor, splits the harness into a runtime layer and a context and orchestration layer. He cites a UC Berkeley study of seven frontier models across harnesses (Pi, Codex, Claude Code) and an Apple and EPFL study finding harness choice did not significantly change coding eval scores, but did change cost per task. His thesis is a data flywheel: harnesses bring harder tasks in reach, usage data flows to labs, and models absorb the skills, so coding harness logic gets deleted; but in new knowledge-work domains (communication, acting versus asking, memory) the harness is adding guardrails back. Parts models cannot absorb are cloud runtime for multi-day tasks, trust and security, and efficiency (cache hit rate, token efficiency, model mix). He predicts 90% of agent work will run off the laptop within six months.

key_facts.quote: the choice of harness did not actually make a difference significantly in the score on SweetBench light
both of those studies actually found that there was a significant difference in cost per task
more coding data is shared with the labs. And eventually the models learn natively how to do these skills as well
curiously in Grockbot, we've actually found ourselves putting back a lot of these things, adding new prompting, adding new guardrails
I predict that within 6 months, 90% of agent work is going to run off the laptop

takeaways: Models absorb harness intelligence via a usage-data flywheel to labs, so harness value shifts to runtime, security and cost efficiency (Q6)
Harness choice moves cost per task more than accuracy, making efficiency the defensible harness-infra wedge (Q11)
Harness logic for non-coding knowledge work is still growing, the window where orchestration vendors can win (Q7)

title: Tied Terms of Service: per-resolution billing, void windows and resolution classes
summary: A real published contract for per-resolution agent billing. A Billable Resolution needs a positive signal: Tier 1 end-user confirmation, Tier 2 system-verified outcome in a connected system, or Tier 3 corroborated silence meeting three conditions; uncorroborated silence, abandonment, negative CSAT, human-touched conversations and escalations never bill. Resolutions are classed (knowledge, read, write_simple, write_financial, orchestrated, long_horizon_case) from the action audit trail. A resolution is voided and credited automatically if the user recontacts on the same issue within 30 days or leaves negative feedback. LLM costs pass through separately and are not credited. Invoice disputes within 30 days. Date is the snapshot date, not the ToS effective date.

LLM inference passed through, not credited on voids
